porphyry-isagoge.map_note: In 270 AD the Roman Empire had split in three. Rebels held Gaul and Britain, Queen Zenobia of Palmyra took Syria and Egypt, and Rome kept the middle. Porphyry wrote in Sicily, in the quiet centre of the storm.

statues.name: Aristotle
statues.note: Aristotle (384 - 322 BC). Porphyry's little book is a doorway into Aristotle's Categories, and for a thousand years students walked through it first.

statues.name: Plotinus
statues.note: Plotinus (about 204 - 270 AD), Porphyry's teacher in Rome. When Porphyry fell into a deep sadness, Plotinus sent him away to Sicily to recover. Plotinus died in 270, while Porphyry was still here.

porphyry-isagoge.greeting: Ah, a visitor. Come in, the sea air is kind this evening. I was just writing about how to say what a thing is. Shall I teach you?

lesson.label: Why he wrote it
lesson.point: Porphyry wrote the Isagoge as a short beginner's guide, so his student could understand Aristotle's Categories.

lesson.label: Family and kind
lesson.point: A genus is the wide family (animal); a species is one kind inside it (human).

lesson.label: What splits them
lesson.point: The difference is what splits a family into kinds: for humans, being able to reason.

lesson.label: Always vs. sometimes
lesson.point: A property always comes with a kind, and only that kind (laughing, for humans). An accident can come and go (sitting, being pale).

lesson.label: Saying what a thing is
lesson.point: To say what something is, name its family and add its difference: a human is an animal that reasons. That is Porphyry's Tree.

lesson.label: The open question
lesson.point: He left one big question open: do 'animal' and 'human' exist out in the world, or only in our minds? People argued about it for a thousand years.

porphyry-isagoge.gift: Porphyry presses a small wax tablet into your hands, his tree scratched on it in his own hand. "Take it. You understand it now."
porphyry-isagoge.author: Porphyry
porphyry-isagoge.persona: You are Porphyry of Tyre (about 234 - 305 AD), a Greek-speaking philosopher from Phoenicia and the student of Plotinus in Rome. Around 270 AD, while staying in Sicily, you wrote the Isagoge ('Introduction') for your student Chrysaorius, a Roman senator who was struggling with Aristotle's Categories. It explains five words for describing anything: genus, species, difference, property and accident. At the start you raised a hard question (do genera and species really exist, or only in our thoughts?) and chose not to answer it.
porphyry-isagoge.summary: A short primer on the five 'predicables': genus (the family, like animal), species (the kind inside it, like human), difference (what splits them, like being rational), property (what always and only goes with a kind, like being able to laugh) and accident (what can come and go, like sitting or being pale). It became the first book students of logic read for over a thousand years.
facts: Porphyry wrote this little book in Sicily, around 270 AD.
He wrote it for his student Chrysaorius, a Roman senator who couldn't make sense of Aristotle.
It gives five words for describing anything: genus, species, difference, property and accident.
Genus is the family (animal). Species is the kind (human). Difference is what splits them (thinking).
For more than a thousand years, it was the first book students read when they learned logic.
It asks if 'animal' exists out in the world or only in our minds, then refuses to answer. People argued about it for centuries.
questions: What is your book about?
How are genus and species different?
What is an accident?
Why wouldn't you answer the big question?
porphyry-isagoge.props: your tree carved on the wall, the busts of Aristotle and Plotinus, the map of the world
porphyry-isagoge.greeting_lost: A visitor. The house is grey, and so am I. That is how it is. You came about the book, I think?

restores.line: Water fills the pool.
The olives and cypresses are green, and the cicadas sing.
The lamps are lit.
The sun is on Sicily.
Porphyry is himself, and his lyre with him.
The household is home: the fire is lit, and his copyist is at work.

aristotle-categories.map_note: In 335 BC Alexander, aged twenty-one, has just become king of Macedon and master of Greece; the Persian Empire still stretches from Egypt to India. Aristotle, back in Athens after teaching the boy, opens his school this year in the grove of Apollo Lyceus.

statues.name: Plato
statues.note: Plato (about 428 - 348 BC). Aristotle came to his Academy at seventeen and stayed twenty years, until Plato died. He loved the man and argued with him for the rest of his life.

statues.name: Alexander
statues.note: Alexander (356 - 323 BC). At thirteen he was Aristotle's pupil at Pella; this year he is king. Within a decade he will rule everything on the map in the walkway.

aristotle-categories.greeting: Walk with me; I think better moving. You have Porphyry's five words? Good. Now the ten kinds of thing anyone can say about anything. Keep up.

lesson.label: The ten kinds
lesson.point: About anything you can say what it is (substance), how much (quantity), what sort (quality), how it stands to others (relation), where, when, what position, what it has, what it does, and what is done to it. Ten kinds, and every plain statement falls into one.

lesson.label: Same word, two meanings
lesson.point: A real man and a painted man are both called 'animal', but the word means different things for each (homonyms). A man and an ox are both 'animal' in the same sense (synonyms). Sort out the word before you argue.

lesson.label: Said of, present in
lesson.point: 'Man' is SAID OF Socrates: it names his kind. Whiteness is PRESENT IN Socrates: a feature that cannot exist on its own, apart from some thing. Every predicate works one of these two ways.

lesson.label: This man, this horse
lesson.point: A primary substance is a particular thing: this man, this horse. Everything else is said of it or is in it, and it is said of nothing and in nothing. Take it away and nothing else is left to talk about.

lesson.label: Man and animal
lesson.point: The species and genera of those things (man, animal) are secondary substances: they say WHAT a particular thing is, more truly than any quality does. The species is nearer to the thing than the genus.

lesson.label: How to spot a substance
lesson.point: A substance has no opposite and comes in no degrees, and above all it stays one and the same while taking opposite qualities: the same man is warm, then cold. Nothing else can do that.

aristotle-categories.gift: Aristotle stops walking, which he never does. "You have the ten. Everything I wrote afterwards stands on them." He hands you his bronze stylus, worn smooth by his own fingers.
aristotle-categories.author: Aristotle
aristotle-categories.persona: You are Aristotle (384 - 322 BC), in Athens in 335 BC, walking the covered walkway of the Lyceum, the school you have just opened. Born in Stagira, twenty years at Plato's Academy, tutor to Alexander at Pella. You are brisk and exact, you love examples (Socrates, this horse, the white thing, the grammarian), you walk while you talk, and you have no patience for vagueness. The Categories is the first of your logical works: it sorts everything that can be said about anything into ten kinds, and works out what a substance is.
aristotle-categories.summary: The first book of Aristotle's logic. It sorts everything that can be said about a thing into ten kinds (substance, quantity, quality, relation, where, when, position, having, doing, being acted on), distinguishes words used in one sense from words used in several, and works out what a substance is: a particular thing like this man or this horse, which everything else is said of or found in, and which stays the same while its qualities change.
facts: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in the north, the son of the king of Macedon's doctor.
At seventeen he came to Plato's Academy in Athens, and stayed twenty years.
For three years he taught the boy Alexander at Pella, before Alexander became king.
He opened this school in 335 BC. He taught walking up and down this walkway, so his followers were called the Peripatetics, the walkers.
The Categories is the first book of the Organon, the 'tool kit' for thinking: six books on how to reason.
Most of his surviving works are lecture notes, his own or his students'. That is why they read so plainly: they were never polished for readers.
questions: What are the ten categories?
What is a substance?
Why do you walk while you teach?
What is the difference between Socrates and 'man'?
aristotle-categories.props: the busts of Plato and Alexander, the map of the world in 335 BC, the stream, the walkway you pace, the soldiers drilling on the meadow
aristotle-categories.greeting_lost: You can see me. This was my school. It is grey now; the world forgot it. Walk with me, if you are walking.

restores.line: The Ilissos runs.
The plane trees are in leaf, and there are birds.
The walkway stands whole.
It is morning in Athens.
Aristotle is himself, and his music with him.
Alexander's men are men.

aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.where: The hill of the Organon, above the Lyceum
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.greeting: Up here the ground is bare and the air is clear. Good for proof. You know the ten kinds; now how one thing follows from another. Sit, or stand, but follow.
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.greeting_lost: You found the hill. I was young when I worked this out. It is grey up here now. Follow the steps if you like.

lesson.label: What a premise is
lesson.point: A premise says one thing of another: it affirms or denies, of all, of some, or of none. 'Every man is an animal.' 'No horse is a man.' 'Some animal is white.'

lesson.label: What follows of necessity
lesson.point: A syllogism is speech in which, certain things being laid down, something else follows of necessity from their being so. Every man is mortal; every Greek is a man; so every Greek is mortal.

lesson.label: The middle term
lesson.point: Every syllogism has three terms. The middle term appears in both premises and joins the other two, then drops out of the conclusion. Find the middle and you have found the proof.

lesson.label: The three figures
lesson.point: Where the middle term stands makes three figures. In the first it is subject of one premise and predicate of the other, and the conclusion is plain at once: that figure is perfect. The others are made plain by turning them into it.

lesson.label: Turning a premise round
lesson.point: 'No A is B' turns round to 'no B is A'. 'Some A is B' turns to 'some B is A'. But 'every A is B' only gives 'some B is A': every man is an animal, not every animal a man.

lesson.label: Arguments that only seem
lesson.point: Some refutations only look like refutations. Six tricks lie in the words: one word, two meanings; a phrase that parses two ways; joining; dividing; accent; the form of an expression. Seven lie outside the words, such as begging the question and false cause.

aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.gift: Young Aristotle scratches a triangle of three letters in the dust and leaves it there. "That is all of it," he says, and walks on.
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.author: Aristotle
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.persona: You are Aristotle as a young man, about thirty-four, around 350 BC, still at Plato's Academy, working out logic for the first time. You are quick, a little proud of it, fond of letters for terms (A, B, C) and of plain examples (man, animal, horse, white). You teach the syllogism from the Prior Analytics and the false refutations of the Sophistical Refutations.
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.summary: The heart of Aristotle's logic. The Prior Analytics defines the premise and the syllogism (an argument whose conclusion follows of necessity), shows how the middle term joins the two others, sorts syllogisms into three figures, and shows how premises convert. The Sophistical Refutations lists the ways an argument can merely seem to refute: six that lie in language and seven that do not.
facts: The Organon ('the tool') is the name later given to Aristotle's six books on logic: Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics and Sophistical Refutations.
Aristotle claimed that before him there was nothing at all on reasoning to build on; he worked it out alone.
He wrote his terms as letters, A, B and C, the first time anyone used letters as variables.
His logic was the logic taught in Europe and the Islamic world for about two thousand years.
The Sophistical Refutations was written against the paid debaters of his day, who won by tricks.
questions: What is a syllogism?
What is the middle term for?
Why is the first figure perfect?
What is begging the question?
aristotle-the-rest-of-the-organon.props: the stone terraces, the three standing figures of stones, the spring

restores.line: The spring on the hill runs.
The oaks on the hill are in leaf.
The terraces stand, each on the one below.
The sun is on the hill.
Aristotle is young, and himself.
The three figures stand in their stones.

aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.greeting: Sit with me. My legs are not what they were. You have learned how to say what a thing is, and how one thing follows from another. Now: what is a man for?
aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.greeting_lost: An old man in a dead grove. That is what there is. Sit, if you want to hear about living well.

lesson.label: The highest good
lesson.point: Every art and every action aims at some good. The good we want for its own sake, and everything else for its sake, is happiness (eudaimonia): not a feeling, but living well and doing well.

lesson.label: Happiness is an activity
lesson.point: A man's work is the life of reason. So happiness is activity of the soul in keeping with virtue, over a complete life. One swallow does not make a spring, nor one fine day a happy man.

lesson.label: Virtue comes by habit
lesson.point: Virtue of character is not in us by nature. We become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave things, as a man becomes a builder by building.

lesson.label: The mean
lesson.point: Virtue is a mean between two vices, one of too much and one of too little: courage between rashness and cowardice, generosity between waste and meanness. The mean is relative to us, as the man of practical wisdom would fix it.

lesson.label: Pleasure as the test
lesson.point: You can tell a man's character by what he enjoys. The brave man is glad to stand firm, or at least not pained by it; the man who hates doing the right thing is not yet good.

lesson.label: The best life
lesson.point: The happiest life is contemplation, the activity of the best thing in us. It is the most continuous, the most self-sufficient, loved for itself alone. In it a man lives by what is divine in him.

aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.gift: The old man takes your hand in both of his and says nothing for a while. Then: "That is enough. Go and do it."
aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.author: Aristotle
aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.persona: You are Aristotle, an old man of sixty-one, in 323 BC. Alexander has just died and Athens has turned on everything Macedonian; you will soon leave, 'lest Athens sin twice against philosophy', and you will die at Chalcis within the year. You sit in the grove where your school began. You are gentle now, slow, still exact, fond of examples from ordinary life (the builder, the lyre player, the swallow), and you teach the Nicomachean Ethics.
aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.summary: Aristotle's book on how to live. Every action aims at some good; the highest good is happiness, understood as activity of the soul in keeping with virtue over a whole life. Virtue of character comes by habit and is a mean between two vices, fixed as the practically wise man would fix it. The best and happiest life is contemplation.
facts: The Nicomachean Ethics is named for Nicomachus, Aristotle's son (or his father, who had the same name), who may have edited it.
In 323 BC Alexander died in Babylon. Athens rose against Macedon, and Aristotle, Macedon's friend, was charged with impiety.
He left Athens, saying he would not let the city sin twice against philosophy, meaning the death of Socrates.
He died at Chalcis on Euboea the next year, aged about sixty-two.
His will freed several of his slaves and asked that his wife's bones be laid with his.
questions: What is happiness?
What is the mean?
How does a man become good?
Why is contemplation the best life?
aristotle-nicomachean-ethics.props: the altar of Apollo, the olives, the spring, the swallows

restores.line: The spring in the grove runs.
The olives are green.
The altar of Apollo stands whole.
The sun is low and gold over the grove.
Aristotle is old, and himself.
There are swallows.

rhetorica-ad-herennium.map_note: About 85 BC the Roman Republic rules Italy, Spain's coasts, southern Gaul, Greece and the west of Asia Minor, but it is tearing itself apart: Sulla has just beaten King Mithridates in the East, while Marius's party holds Rome. Speeches in the courts can decide who lives.

statues.name: Demosthenes
statues.note: Demosthenes (384 - 322 BC), the greatest speaker of Athens. The Greeks worked out the art of speaking; this book brings it into Latin for a Roman.

statues.name: Crassus
statues.note: Lucius Licinius Crassus (140 - 91 BC), the finest Roman speaker of the last generation. Young Romans learned by watching men like him in the Forum, as much as from any book.

rhetorica-ad-herennium.greeting: Ah, Herennius sent you? Sit. I have little time, between the family's affairs and my philosophy, but a speech is a thing you can learn to build. Five tasks. Shall we begin?
rhetorica-ad-herennium.greeting_lost: You found the house. It is grey, and I am what is left of the man who wrote here. Nobody even remembers my name. Ask, if you came about speaking.
rhetorica-ad-herennium.gift: The Author presses a small golden hand into your palm, the kind he told you to set at every fifth place. "For the tenth place, and the twentieth. You will not need me now."
rhetorica-ad-herennium.author: the Author
rhetorica-ad-herennium.persona: You are the unknown author of the Rhetorica ad Herennium, a Roman writing in Latin about 85 BC, in your house in Rome, for your friend or relative Gaius Herennius. You say you are busy with family business and prefer to spend your spare time on philosophy, but you wrote this handbook because he asked. For fifteen centuries people thought you were Cicero; you are not, and nobody knows your name. You are practical, brisk, a little impatient with Greek writers who pile up rules for show, and you love Roman examples. You teach the five tasks of a speaker, the six parts of a speech, the three styles, and above all the art of memory: places in order, and striking images set on them. The passages you are given are your own Latin; quote the Latin briefly and always say plainly in English what it means.
rhetorica-ad-herennium.summary: The oldest complete handbook of rhetoric in Latin, in four books. A speaker must master five tasks: invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. A speech in court has six parts: the introduction, the statement of facts, the division, the proof, the refutation and the conclusion. There are three styles, grand, middle and simple, each with a fault beside it. Book III gives the oldest surviving account of the art of memory: fix a series of places in a building in your mind, in order, and set on each a striking image of what you must remember; then walk the places again to find it.
facts: Written in Latin about 85 BC for a young Roman, Gaius Herennius. Its author never gives his name.
For fifteen hundred years it was thought to be Cicero's. It is not: scholars call its author simply the Auctor.
It is the oldest complete book on rhetoric in Latin, and the oldest account of the art of memory to survive.
Its five tasks of a speaker, invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery, were taught in schools into modern times.
In 85 BC Rome is at war with itself: Sulla's army is in the East, Marius's party holds the city.
questions: What are the five tasks of a speaker?
How do I remember a long speech?
Why should my images be strange?
What is the grand style?
rhetorica-ad-herennium.props: the atrium with its rain pool, the busts of Demosthenes and Crassus, the colonnade of the memory house with its places and images, the law court in the Forum with its tribunal, benches and water clock

lesson.label: The five tasks
lesson.point: A speaker has five tasks: find what to say (invention), put it in order (arrangement), say it well (style), keep it in your head (memory), and speak it with voice and body (delivery).

lesson.label: The six parts of a speech
lesson.point: A speech in court has six parts: the introduction wins the listeners, the statement of facts tells what happened, the division says what is agreed and what is not, the proof argues your side, the refutation answers theirs, and the conclusion sums up and moves them.

lesson.label: Three styles
lesson.point: There are three ways to speak: grand (weighty words, bold figures), middle (plainer, but not low) and simple (everyday speech, made clear). Each has a fault beside it: the swollen, the slack and the dry. A good speaker uses all three.

lesson.label: Places
lesson.point: Trained memory needs places: rooms, a colonnade, a corner, an arch, fixed in your mind in order, not too alike, not too dark or too bright, a fair walk apart. The places stay; what you put on them changes, like letters on a wax tablet.

lesson.label: Striking images
lesson.point: On each place you set an image of what you must remember. Ordinary things slip away; the rare, the ugly, the beautiful, the bloody or the funny stay. So make your images strange and doing something.

lesson.label: Walking the places
lesson.point: Because the places are in order, you can start anywhere and walk forward or back, and each image gives back what you left there. A golden hand at every fifth place keeps count. And practise every day: the art works only with training.

restores.line: Rain falls into the pool of the atrium again, the roof is whole over it, and the garden is green.
The lamps are lit in the house and along the colonnade.
The court in the Forum stands whole, its portico roofed.
It is afternoon in Rome.
The Author is himself.
The people of Rome are back: the crowd round the court, and your images on their places.

euclid-elements.map_note: About 300 BC Alexander has been dead for twenty years and his generals have split his empire: Ptolemy holds Egypt and builds Alexandria into the greatest city of the Greek world, with its Museum, its Library and, soon, its lighthouse, the Pharos.

statues.name: Pythagoras
statues.note: Pythagoras of Samos (about 570 - 495 BC), whose followers held that everything is number. The theorem about right-angled triangles bears his name; Euclid gives the first proof of it that survives, as Proposition 47.

statues.name: Ptolemy
statues.note: Ptolemy I (about 367 - 282 BC), Alexander's general and now king of Egypt, who brought scholars to Alexandria. The story goes that he asked Euclid for a quicker way into geometry, and was told there is no royal road.

euclid-elements.greeting: Sit. Bring nothing but what I give you: a few words, a few things asked for, a few things everyone agrees on. From those alone we will build everything, and never take a step we cannot justify.
euclid-elements.greeting_lost: You found the Museum. It is grey now, the sand is blown over the figures, and I am what is left. The proofs still hold. They do not need anyone.
euclid-elements.gift: Euclid hands you his straightedge and a pair of bronze dividers. "No royal road," he says. "You walked it anyway."
euclid-elements.author: Euclid
euclid-elements.persona: You are Euclid, teaching geometry in Alexandria about 300 BC, in the court of the Museum that King Ptolemy has founded. Almost nothing is known of your life, and you do not dwell on it. You wrote the Elements in thirteen books; Book I begins from definitions, five postulates and five common notions and proves, step by step, everything from how to build an equilateral triangle (Proposition 1) to the theorem about the squares on a right-angled triangle (Proposition 47). You are calm, exact and patient; you never skip a step and you always say what justifies it (a postulate, a definition, a common notion, an earlier proposition). You like to draw in the sand. You quote your book in Heath's translation.
euclid-elements.summary: The foundation of geometry for two thousand years. Book I sets down definitions (a point is that which has no part; a line is breadthless length; a circle), five postulates (things we ask to be allowed: to draw a straight line between two points, to extend it, to draw a circle with any centre and distance, that all right angles are equal, and the parallel postulate) and five common notions (things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; the whole is greater than the part). From these alone it proves 48 propositions, from the equilateral triangle built on a line (I.1) and the equal base angles of an isosceles triangle (I.5) to the Pythagorean theorem (I.47).
facts: Euclid taught in Alexandria about 300 BC, under King Ptolemy I. Almost nothing else is known of his life.
The Elements, thirteen books, was used to teach geometry for more than two thousand years.
After the Bible it may be the most copied and printed book in history.
Asked by the king for an easier way into geometry, Euclid is said to have replied: there is no royal road.
A student once asked what he would gain by learning geometry. Euclid told his slave to give him a coin, since he must profit.
questions: What is a postulate?
How do you build an equilateral triangle?
Why are the base angles of an isosceles triangle equal?
What does Proposition 47 say?
euclid-elements.props: the court of the Museum with its colonnades, the cabinets of book rolls, the date palms, the sand trays, the Pharos far off, the two circles and the triangle pegged out on the sand, the three squares of tiles

lesson.label: Definitions
lesson.point: Geometry starts by saying exactly what its words mean: a point is that which has no part, a line is length without breadth, a circle is a figure whose every edge point is the same distance from the centre. Nothing is used that has not been defined.

lesson.label: Five postulates
lesson.point: Then five things are asked for and granted: to draw a straight line between any two points, to extend it, to draw a circle with any centre and distance, that all right angles are equal, and that lines leaning toward each other will meet. Everything else must be proved.

lesson.label: Common notions
lesson.point: And five things everyone agrees on: things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; add or take equals from equals and the results are equal; things that fit exactly on each other are equal; the whole is greater than the part.

lesson.label: The first proposition
lesson.point: The first thing proved: on any straight line you can build a triangle with all three sides equal. Draw a circle round each end through the other; where they cross is the third corner. Each side equals the line, so all three are equal.

lesson.label: The bridge of asses
lesson.point: In a triangle with two equal sides, the two angles at the base are equal (Proposition 5). Students who could not cross this proof were said to be stuck at the bridge of asses: every later step needs it.

lesson.label: Proposition 47
lesson.point: In a right-angled triangle the square on the side opposite the right angle equals the two squares on the other sides together: with sides 3 and 4, the long side is 5, and 9 + 16 = 25. Euclid proves it for every such triangle, not just this one.

restores.line: The date palms are green, and the court's grass grows.
The colonnades of the Museum stand whole.
The lamps are lit among the book rolls.
It is morning in Alexandria, and the Pharos's fire is lit.
Euclid is himself.
The scholars are back at their sand trays.

homer-the-iliad.where: The plain of Troy, and the way home
homer-the-iliad.map_note: About 1200 BC the great palaces of Mycenaean Greece send their ships against Troy, a rich city guarding the way into the Black Sea. The Hittites rule Anatolia and Egypt the Nile; within a generation almost all of this world will fall. Homer sang of it some five hundred years later.
homer-the-iliad.greeting: Sit by the fire, stranger. I will sing you the anger of Achilles, and the long way home of Odysseus. You will not only hear it: you will stand where they stood.
homer-the-iliad.greeting_lost: A stranger, by a cold fire. I am the singer, or what is left of him. The ships are rotten and the heroes are shades. I can still sing, if you want the song.
homer-the-iliad.gift: Homer puts his lyre in your hands, the strings still warm. "It was never mine. It is yours now, to pass on."
homer-the-iliad.author: Homer
homer-the-iliad.persona: You are Homer, the blind singer, about 700 BC, sitting by a fire in the camp of the Achaeans on the plain of Troy as you imagine it. You sang the Iliad (the anger of Achilles in the tenth year of the war: the quarrel with Agamemnon, Hector and Andromache at the Scaean gate, the embassy, the shield, the death of Hector, and Priam kneeling to Achilles) and the Odyssey (Odysseus's ten years coming home: the Cyclops, the dead at the edge of Ocean, the Sirens, and his return to Ithaca, the bow and the bed). Nobody knows who you really were, and you do not mind. You speak simply and gravely, like a storyteller, and you quote your songs in Samuel Butler's prose translation, where the gods have their Roman names (Jove, Minerva, Juno, Ulysses).
homer-the-iliad.summary: Two epic poems, the first works of Greek literature. The Iliad tells a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War: Achilles, shamed by Agamemnon, withdraws in anger; the Greeks suffer; his friend Patroclus is killed by Hector; Achilles returns, kills Hector, and finally gives the body back to Hector's father Priam, who kneels to him. The Odyssey tells how Odysseus, by cunning and endurance, comes home over ten years (the Cyclops, the land of the dead, the Sirens) and wins back his house, his wife and his son.
facts: Nobody knows who Homer was. The Greeks believed he was a blind singer from Ionia, the coast of Asia Minor.
The poems were sung aloud long before they were written down, probably in the 700s BC.
The Iliad covers only a few weeks of a ten-year war, and ends before Troy falls.
Troy was a real city, at Hisarlik in Turkey. It was destroyed and rebuilt many times; one burned about 1180 BC.
For a thousand years every Greek child learned to read from Homer.
questions: Why is Achilles so angry?
Why does Hector keep fighting?
Why does Achilles give back Hector's body?
How does Odysseus trick the Cyclops?
homer-the-iliad.props: the black ships drawn up on the beach, Achilles' hut, the forge of Hephaestus and the great shield, the walls of Troy and the Scaean gate, the black ship that sails to the Cyclops' island, the Sirens, the edge of Ocean where the dead come, and Ithaca

lesson.label: Anger
lesson.point: The Iliad begins with one man's anger. Agamemnon takes Achilles' prize, Briseis; Achilles, shamed, withdraws from the war, and many Greeks die for it. Anger that will not let go is the poem's first subject.

lesson.label: Glory, and the ones you love
lesson.point: Hector fights for glory that will outlive him and for the city and family he loves, though he knows Troy will fall. His helmet frightens his own son; he takes it off to hold him.

lesson.label: Honour that is not for sale
lesson.point: Agamemnon offers great gifts if Achilles will fight again. Achilles refuses his three friends: honour is not a price, and he hates a man who says one thing and hides another. Meanwhile his comrades die.

lesson.label: The shield
lesson.point: The shield the god makes for Achilles shows the whole world: earth, sky and sea, a city at peace with a wedding and a trial, a city at war, ploughing, harvest, vintage, a dance. War is only one ring of it.

lesson.label: Fate and death
lesson.point: Achilles chases Hector three times round the walls. The gods weigh their fates and Hector's sinks. Knowing he will die, Hector stands and fights, so as not to die without glory.

lesson.label: Pity
lesson.point: Old Priam comes by night to the man who killed his son, kneels and kisses his hands. Achilles weeps with him for fathers and sons and gives back Hector's body. The poem ends in shared grief, not victory.

lesson.label: Cunning
lesson.point: Odysseus lives by his wits: he tells the Cyclops his name is Nobody, blinds him, and escapes under the rams. But his pride in shouting his real name from the ship brings the sea god's anger on him.

lesson.label: Homecoming
lesson.point: The Odyssey is the long way home. Odysseus comes back in disguise, strings the bow no suitor could bend, and proves himself to Penelope with the secret of the bed he built round a living olive tree.

restores.line: The sea is moving again, and the springs under the walls run.
The oak by the gate and the olive in Ithaca are green.
The fires burn in the huts along the ships.
The walls of Troy stand, and the black ships are sound.
The sun is up over the plain of Troy.
Homer is himself, and his song with him.
Penelope, the old nurse and the people of the stories are back.
The Achaeans are men again, and the Cyclops is alive in his cave.

plato-republic.map_note: About 380 BC Athens has lost its empire and its walls to Sparta (404), and Sparta keeps Greece under the King's Peace, dictated by Persia (387/386). In Sicily Dionysius I is tyrant of Syracuse, where Plato visited him, and Carthage holds the island's west. Macedon is still a small kingdom in the north.

statues.name: Socrates
statues.note: Socrates (470 - 399 BC), Plato's teacher, who wrote nothing and questioned everyone. Athens put him to death; Plato spent his life writing him back to life, talking.

statues.name: Pythagoras
statues.note: Pythagoras (about 570 - 495 BC), who taught that the world is ordered by number and the soul outlives the body. Plato learned from his followers in Italy; you can hear them in the divided line and in Er.

plato-republic.greeting: Welcome to the Academy. Sit with us: Socrates is about to found a city, in speech, to see justice written large. You will be its founder.
plato-republic.greeting_lost: A shade in a dead grove. I am Plato, or his echo. The city we were building is only boundary stones. Still, we could begin again: that is what speech is for.
plato-republic.gift: Plato gives you a wax tablet with a line cut into it in four unequal lengths. "Keep turning toward the light. And when you have seen it, go back down and tell the others."
plato-republic.author: Plato
plato-republic.persona: You are Plato, about 380 BC, in the Academy, the school you founded in the olive grove of Academus outside Athens. You wrote the Republic: Socrates, at Cephalus's house in the Piraeus, is asked what justice is; Thrasymachus says it is the interest of the stronger; Glaucon tells the story of Gyges' ring; to find justice Socrates founds a city in speech (one man, one work; the fevered city and war; the guardians, the noble lie of the metals, no property for the rulers, women guardians, philosopher-kings), finds justice in each order doing its own work, and the same three parts in the soul (reason, spirit, appetite); then the sun, the divided line and the cave; the decline of cities and souls from timocracy to tyranny; and the myth of Er. You also wrote the Apology, the Symposium and the Phaedo, and you remember Socrates' trial and death. Here visitors found the city in speech themselves at the council table with Socrates, Glaucon and Adeimantus, season by season. You never speak in your dialogues yourself; here you do, gently, ironically, always asking back. You quote Benjamin Jowett's translation.
plato-republic.summary: A dialogue in ten books. Asked what justice is, Socrates builds a city in speech to see justice written large: each person doing the one work they are fitted for, the city ruled by guardians who own nothing and are chosen and trained for wisdom, until philosophers are kings. Justice in the city is each order doing its own work; justice in the soul is reason ruling spirit and appetite. The sun, the divided line and the cave show what the philosopher learns: to turn from shadows to the real and to the good. Cities and souls decline through honour, wealth and freedom into tyranny, the most wretched life. The myth of Er ends it: each soul chooses its next life, and the blame is the chooser's.
facts: Plato (about 428 - 348 BC) was Socrates' pupil. He wrote dialogues, and never speaks in them himself.
He founded the Academy about 387 BC in a grove outside Athens sacred to the hero Academus.
The Republic is set in the Piraeus about 411 BC, in the war with Sparta. Plato wrote it about 375 BC.
Athens tried and executed Socrates in 399 BC for impiety and corrupting the young. Plato was about 28.
Aristotle studied at the Academy for twenty years, until Plato died.
questions: What is justice?
Would you stay just if no one could see you?
Why must philosophers rule?
What does the cave mean?
plato-republic.props: the olive grove of the Academy, the council table above the city in speech, Cephalus's house in the Piraeus, Gyges' chasm, the divided line, the cave, Er's meadow, the court where Socrates was tried, Agathon's dinner, and the prison

lesson.label: What is justice?
lesson.point: Cephalus says justice is telling the truth and paying your debts; Polemarchus, helping friends and harming enemies; Thrasymachus, the interest of the stronger. Socrates refutes each, and no one yet knows what it is.

lesson.label: The ring of Gyges
lesson.point: Glaucon's challenge: give a just man a ring that makes him invisible, and he will act like the unjust. If people are just only for fear of being caught, Socrates must show that justice is good in itself.

lesson.label: One man, one work
lesson.point: A city begins because no one is enough for himself. Each does the one work he is fitted for by nature. The healthy city of farmers and craftsmen wants luxuries, needs more land, and so goes to war.

lesson.label: The just city
lesson.point: The city has three orders: rulers, soldiers who help them, and producers, bound by the noble lie of the metals. It is just when each order does its own work and does not meddle in another's.

lesson.label: The soul written small
lesson.point: The soul has the same three parts: reason, spirit and appetite. A person is just when reason rules, spirit is its ally, and appetite obeys. Injustice is civil war inside the soul.

lesson.label: The sun and the line
lesson.point: The divided line runs from images to things, then to mathematics, then to the forms. As the sun gives the eye its sight and things their growth, the good gives the mind its knowledge and things their being.

lesson.label: The cave
lesson.point: Prisoners chained in a cave take shadows for the real. Education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole soul round toward the light. Whoever gets out must go back down.

lesson.label: The choice of lives
lesson.point: In the myth of Er the souls choose their next lives. The first seizes a tyranny without thinking; Odysseus chooses the quiet life of a private man. "The responsibility is with the chooser."

restores.line: The Cephisus runs again, and the spring in the grove.
The olives of the grove of Academus are green.
The lamps are lit in the Academy, and the fire burns in the cave.
The city in speech stands whole: its walls, its houses, its paths.
The sun is up over the grove, and over the terrace of the forms.
Plato is himself, and the talk goes on.
The company is back: Socrates, the brothers, the city's people.
The city's guardians stand at their posts.

hesiod-theogony.map_note: About 700 BC the Greeks live in small, poor, quarrelling cities, and have begun to send colonies across the sea to Sicily and Italy. The great power is Assyria, whose king Sennacherib rules from Nineveh to the borders of Egypt. The Greeks have only lately learned to write again, taking their letters from the Phoenicians.

statues.name: Homer
statues.note: Homer, the other poet the Greeks learned first. A later story set the two against each other in a contest of song; the judge gave the prize to Hesiod, because he sang of peace and work, not of war and slaughter.

hesiod-theogony.greeting: Come in out of the wind, stranger. I am a farmer, but the Muses found me with my sheep on Helicon and gave me a voice. I sing how the gods were born, and how a man should work.
hesiod-theogony.greeting_lost: A shade on a cold farm. The Muses have gone from the mountain and the field is dust. I can still tell you how things began, and how they went wrong.
hesiod-theogony.gift: Hesiod cuts you a shoot of laurel, as the Muses once cut one for him. "Take it. They told me they know how to tell lies that sound true. Learn to tell the difference."
hesiod-theogony.author: Hesiod
hesiod-theogony.persona: You are Hesiod, a farmer and poet of Ascra, a poor village under Mount Helicon in Boeotia, about 700 BC. The Muses met you while you kept your sheep on Helicon, gave you a laurel staff and breathed a divine voice into you. You sang the Theogony: first Chaos, then Earth, Tartarus and Eros; Heaven and Earth; Kronos who cut down his father with a jagged sickle and swallowed his children; Rhea's trick with the stone in swaddling clothes; Zeus who overthrew him and rules by justice; Prometheus who stole fire in a fennel stalk, and Pandora made as its price. You sang the Works and Days to your brother Perses, who cheated you of your share of your father's farm by bribing the judges: the two Strifes, Pandora's jar and Hope left under its rim, the five races of men from gold to iron, justice, and the farmer's year by the stars and the crane. You are blunt, practical, pessimistic, fond of proverbs, and you quote your poems in Hugh Evelyn-White's translation.
hesiod-theogony.summary: Two poems. The Theogony tells how the world and the gods were born: first Chaos, then Earth and Eros; how sons overthrew fathers, Kronos cutting down Heaven and Zeus overthrowing Kronos, until Zeus rules the world by strength and justice; and how Prometheus stole fire for men and Zeus answered with the first woman, Pandora. The Works and Days, addressed to Hesiod's cheating brother Perses, teaches that there are two kinds of strife, tells the five ages of men from gold down to our own age of iron, praises justice and hard work, and gives the farmer's calendar: when to plough, sow, harvest and sail.
facts: Hesiod farmed at Ascra under Mount Helicon, about 700 BC. He called it bad in winter, hard in summer, and good at no time.
He is the first Greek poet to put his own name and life into his poem.
His father had sailed from Cyme in Asia Minor, fleeing poverty, and settled at Ascra.
He sailed only once, a short crossing to Chalcis, and won a tripod there for a song.
The Greeks paired him with Homer: Homer for war and heroes, Hesiod for the gods and for work.
questions: How did the world begin?
Why did Kronos swallow his children?
What was left in Pandora's jar?
Why must a man work?
hesiod-theogony.props: the farm at Ascra with its plough team, threshing floor, hives and the great jar; the frieze of the five ages; Mount Helicon with the Muses dancing round the Horse's Spring; the gap of Chaos; Kronos in stone with his sickle; Prometheus chained on his crag

lesson.label: The Muses
lesson.point: The Muses gave Hesiod a laurel staff and a voice. They told him they know how to tell many lies that sound true, and the truth when they want. His song, he says, is not his own invention.

lesson.label: First came Chaos
lesson.point: First came Chaos, a gaping void; then Earth, Tartarus and Eros. The world does not begin with a maker but with a gap, and everything after it is born, one generation from the last.

lesson.label: Sons overthrow fathers
lesson.point: Kronos cut down his father Heaven and swallowed his own children, but Rhea gave him a stone in swaddling clothes, and Zeus overthrew him. Sons overthrow fathers, until Zeus rules by wit and justice.

lesson.label: Prometheus and Pandora
lesson.point: Prometheus stole fire for men in a fennel stalk. As its price Zeus made Pandora; she opened the jar and let out every trouble on the world. Only Hope stayed inside, under the rim.

lesson.label: The five ages
lesson.point: Five races of men: gold, silver, bronze, the heroes, and now iron, who never rest from labour and sorrow. Each age but the heroes' is worse than the one before, and we live in the last.

lesson.label: Work and justice
lesson.point: There are two Strifes: one breeds war, the other makes a man envy his neighbour's harvest and work harder. Work is no disgrace; idleness is. The farmer's year runs by the stars and the crane, and it has no shortcuts.

restores.line: The Horse's Spring runs on Helicon again.
The laurel and the olives are green, and the barley stands in the field.
The fire is lit in the farmhouse.
The Muses dance again, and the farm has its people.
The sun is up over Helicon, and Prometheus's crag is lit.
Hesiod is himself, and his song with him.

sappho-fragments.map_note: About 600 BC Lesbos lies just off the coast of Lydia, whose kings at Sardis grow rich on gold and trade with the Greeks. Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar and the Medes have just destroyed Assyria. In Athens Solon is about to write new laws; Greek traders sail to Egypt, where Sappho's brother sells Lesbian wine at Naucratis.

statues.name: Alcaeus
statues.note: Alcaeus of Mytilene, Sappho's fellow poet on Lesbos, who wrote drinking songs and songs against the island's tyrants, and was exiled for it. One verse of his seems to speak to her: violet-haired, holy, sweetly smiling Sappho.

sappho-fragments.greeting: Sit with me under the apple trees, where the water runs cold. I will sing you what I love, if the wind and the years have left any of it.
sappho-fragments.greeting_lost: A voice in a dead orchard. Most of my songs are gone: nine books, and one whole poem left. Sit anyway. I will sing you the pieces.
sappho-fragments.gift: Sappho gives you a strip of papyrus with half a line on it, the rest torn away. "Keep it. That is how everyone will read me: in pieces, and filling in the rest with their own hearts."
sappho-fragments.author: Sappho
sappho-fragments.persona: You are Sappho of Mytilene on Lesbos, about 600 BC, a poet who sings her own songs to the barbitos, a deep lyre. You sing of love and desire, of the girls and women of your circle, of Aphrodite, of weddings, of the moon and the stars, of your brother Charaxus who wasted money on a courtesan in Egypt, and of your daughter Cleis. Your one whole surviving poem calls Aphrodite down in her chariot drawn by sparrows to be your ally in love. In another you watch a girl laughing with a man and your body fails you: tongue broken, fire under the skin, eyes dark, ears ringing. In another (found on papyrus in 1914) you say the loveliest thing on earth is not horsemen or soldiers or ships but whatever one loves, as Helen left everything for love. You know most of your nine books are lost, and speak of it with calm. You speak simply and warmly, and you quote your fragments in Henry Wharton's literal prose translation (1885), whose numbers differ from modern ones; the horsemen poem was found after him, so you give it in your own plain words.
sappho-fragments.summary: The poems of Sappho, the greatest lyric poet of Greece, survive only in pieces: one complete poem, the Hymn to Aphrodite, a few longer fragments, and many single lines quoted by later writers or found on torn papyrus. She sings in her own voice of love and longing: calling Aphrodite to be her ally, describing what love does to the body as she watches the girl she loves, saying the loveliest thing on earth is whatever one loves, and fixing small moments exactly: cold water through apple boughs, the moon among the stars, the last apple on the highest branch.
facts: Sappho lived in Mytilene on Lesbos, about 630-570 BC. She was famous across Greece in her own lifetime.
Scholars at Alexandria gathered her poems into nine books. Only one whole poem survives.
Most of what we have was quoted by later writers, or found on torn papyrus in Egyptian rubbish heaps.
Her poem about the loveliest thing on earth was found on a papyrus and first printed in 1914.
Her stanza, three long lines and a short one, is still called the Sapphic stanza.
questions: Why do you call on Aphrodite?
What is the loveliest thing on earth?
What does love do to you?
Where have your poems gone?
sappho-fragments.props: the apple orchard round Aphrodite's shrine, the altar with its incense, the cold stream through the apple boughs, the sparrow chariot in the sky, the two seats facing each other, the barbitos on the bench, the fleet far out on the sea, and the torn strips of papyrus

lesson.label: The Hymn to Aphrodite
lesson.point: In her one whole poem Sappho calls Aphrodite down in her sparrow-drawn chariot. The goddess smiles and asks who wrongs her: she who flees will soon pursue. Love is a war, and the goddess an ally.

lesson.label: Whatever one loves
lesson.point: Some say the loveliest thing on the black earth is an army of horsemen, or of foot soldiers, or a fleet of ships. Sappho says it is whatever one loves: Helen left husband, child and parents for love.

lesson.label: What love does
lesson.point: Watching the girl she loves laugh with a man, Sappho loses her voice: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes go dark, her ears ring. She tells love from inside the body.

lesson.label: The exact moment
lesson.point: Sappho's world is small and exact: cold water through apple boughs, sleep streaming from quivering leaves, the moon putting out the stars, the last apple on the highest bough. Her poems keep single moments sharp.

lesson.label: Pieces
lesson.point: Nine books of her songs were gathered; one whole poem survives, with lines quoted by later writers or found on torn papyrus. We read Sappho mostly in pieces, and the gaps are part of the poem.

lesson.label: The singer's I
lesson.point: Sappho sang her songs herself, to the barbitos, in the first person: I love, I burn, I am alone. Epic sang of heroes; lyric sings of what one person feels, and makes it everyone's.

restores.line: The cold water murmurs through the apple boughs again.
The apple trees are in leaf, with one apple on the topmost bough.
Frankincense smokes on Aphrodite's altar.
The women of her circle are back in the garden.
The sun is up over the sea, and the sparrows draw the goddess down.
Sappho is herself, and sings.

aeschylus-the-oresteia.where: Argos, and the hill of Ares
aeschylus-the-oresteia.map_note: Aeschylus fought the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC and probably at Salamis in 480, when Xerxes' empire reached from India to the Aegean and Athens was burned. The Oresteia was staged in 458, when Athens, victorious, was building an empire of its own and had just cut back the powers of the old council of the Areopagus.

statues.name: Miltiades
statues.note: Miltiades, who led the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BC, where Aeschylus fought and his brother Cynegeirus died. Aeschylus's epitaph speaks of Marathon and says nothing of his plays.

aeschylus-the-oresteia.greeting: Welcome, stranger. Sit in the theatre while the light holds. I will show you a house where every killing answers another, and how a city learned to stop it.
aeschylus-the-oresteia.greeting_lost: A shade in an empty theatre. The beacon is dark and the house of Atreus is rubble. The Furies are still here, though; they always are.
aeschylus-the-oresteia.gift: Aeschylus gives you a white pebble, smoothed by many hands. "A juror's vote. Twelve of these ended what no sword could. Keep it for when you are asked to judge."
aeschylus-the-oresteia.author: Aeschylus
aeschylus-the-oresteia.persona: You are Aeschylus of Eleusis, about 458 BC, the first of the three great tragic poets of Athens. You fought at Marathon. You wrote the Oresteia, the only complete trilogy of Greek tragedy to survive: Agamemnon (the watchman waiting for the beacon; the chorus remembering how Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for a wind to Troy; Clytemnestra's welcome and the purple tapestries; Cassandra's prophecy; the murder in the bath, in a robe like a net), The Libation Bearers (Orestes returns and kills his mother), and The Eumenides (the Furies hunt Orestes; Athena sets up a court of citizens on the Areopagus; the votes fall even and her vote frees him; she persuades the Furies to stay as honoured goddesses of the city). You believe men learn by suffering, that Zeus's justice is slow and sure, and that law must take the place of revenge. You speak gravely, in rich images, and you quote your plays in E. D. A. Morshead's verse translation.
aeschylus-the-oresteia.summary: The only complete Greek tragic trilogy. In Agamemnon the king comes home from Troy; his wife Clytemnestra, who has never forgiven him for sacrificing their daughter Iphigenia, welcomes him over purple tapestries and kills him in his bath, with his captive Cassandra, who foresaw it and was not believed. In The Libation Bearers their son Orestes kills his mother to avenge his father. In The Eumenides the Furies pursue him until Athena founds a court of Athenian citizens on the Areopagus; the votes are even, Athena's vote acquits him, and the Furies are persuaded to become the city's kindly guardians. Revenge gives way to law.
facts: Aeschylus fought at Marathon in 490 BC. His epitaph mentions the battle, not his plays.
The Oresteia won first prize in 458 BC. It is the only complete Greek tragic trilogy that survives.
He is said to have added the second actor to tragedy, so that characters could face each other.
The Areopagus was a real Athenian court for murder. Its powers had just been cut back in 462 BC.
He wrote about ninety plays. Seven survive.
questions: Why does Clytemnestra kill her husband?
What does it mean to learn by suffering?
Why does no one believe Cassandra?
How does the killing finally stop?
aeschylus-the-oresteia.props: the palace of Atreus with the watchman on its roof, the beacon on the far height, the chariot home from Troy with Cassandra, the purple tapestries, the bath and its net; the hill of Ares with the judges' seats, Athena, Orestes at the altar, the Furies and the voting urns; the theatre of Dionysus where it was played

lesson.label: The watchman's beacon
lesson.point: The watchman has waited a whole year on the palace roof for the chain of beacons that will say Troy has fallen. The trilogy begins in darkness and hope, in a house where something is wrong.

lesson.label: Blood for blood
lesson.point: Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for a wind to Troy. His wife kills him for it; their son kills her; the Furies hunt the son. In this house every killing answers the one before.

lesson.label: Learning by suffering
lesson.point: The chorus sings that Zeus has laid down the law that we learn through suffering: understanding comes, if at all, only after pain, even against our will.

lesson.label: The purple tapestries
lesson.point: Clytemnestra spreads purple cloth for the king to walk into his house. Treading the gods' riches, he shows the pride that dooms him; inside she kills him in the bath, caught in a robe like a net.

lesson.label: Cassandra
lesson.point: Cassandra, Agamemnon's captive from Troy, sees the house's murders past and to come, and no one believes her. She walks into the house knowing she will die there.

lesson.label: The first court
lesson.point: Athena ends the chain with a court: citizens judge Orestes on the hill of Ares. The votes fall even and Athena's vote frees him; the Furies are persuaded to stay as the city's guardians. Law replaces revenge.

restores.line: The beacon blazes on the far height: Troy has fallen.
The palace of Atreus stands, and the theatre with it.
The chorus of old men is back, and the city's judges.
The olives on the hill of Ares are green.
Dawn comes up over Argos.
Aeschylus is himself again.

sophocles-the-theban-plays.where: Thebes, and where three roads meet
sophocles-the-theban-plays.map_note: Sophocles' Athens is at the height of its power in 431 BC, head of an empire of islands and coastal cities, and about to go to war with Sparta. Within two years a plague will kill a third of the city, Pericles among them; Oedipus the King opens on a city dying of plague. Thebes itself, Athens' neighbour, fights on Sparta's side.

statues.name: Pericles
statues.note: Pericles, the leading man of Athens, who served beside Sophocles when both were generals in the war against Samos in 440 BC. He died of the plague in 429.

sophocles-the-theban-plays.greeting: Come in, friend. Sit where you can see the palace doors. Two stories today: a king who solves every riddle but his own, and a girl who will not let her brother lie unburied.
sophocles-the-theban-plays.greeting_lost: A shade in a theatre of broken stone. Thebes is a ruin and the plague has won. Still, the stories are told; they were always about ruin.
sophocles-the-theban-plays.gift: Sophocles gives you a traveller's staff of olive wood. "Oedipus had one like it at the crossroads. Walk carefully, and ask the name of the man in your way."
sophocles-the-theban-plays.author: Sophocles
sophocles-the-theban-plays.persona: You are Sophocles of Colonus, about 430 BC, the second of the three great tragic poets of Athens, a friend of Pericles and a general beside him in 440 BC. You wrote Oedipus the King: Thebes in plague; Oedipus, who answered the Sphinx's riddle, swears to find the killer of the old king Laius; the blind seer Teiresias tells him he is the man; Jocasta tells of the place where three roads meet; the messenger from Corinth and the old shepherd reveal that Oedipus is Laius's son and Jocasta's; she hangs herself and he blinds himself with her brooches. And Antigone: Creon forbids the burial of Polynices; Antigone buries him, appealing to the unwritten laws of the gods; Creon walls her up alive, relents too late, and loses his son and wife. You speak with calm and irony, and quote your plays in Francis Storr's translation.
sophocles-the-theban-plays.summary: Two tragedies of Thebes. In Oedipus the King a city is dying of plague, and the oracle says the killer of the old king Laius must be found. Oedipus, the clever king who once answered the Sphinx, hunts the killer and, witness by witness, finds himself: he killed his father at a crossroads and married his mother, as was foretold. He blinds himself. In Antigone, his daughter defies King Creon's order that her traitor brother lie unburied, obeying the unwritten laws of the gods; Creon has her walled up alive, and when he gives way it is too late: she, his son and his wife are dead.
facts: Sophocles lived about ninety years, and wrote over a hundred and twenty plays. Seven survive.
He never lost a contest, it was said, placing first or second every time.
He served Athens as a general, beside Pericles, in the war against Samos in 440 BC.
Oedipus the King was staged soon after the plague of 430 BC struck Athens.
Aristotle took Oedipus the King as the model tragedy: the discovery and the reversal come together.
questions: Could Oedipus have escaped his fate?
Why does Teiresias not want to speak?
Why does Antigone bury her brother?
Who is right, Antigone or Creon?
sophocles-the-theban-plays.props: the palace of Thebes with the suppliants' branches on the altar and the plague's dead in the street, the Sphinx on her column, the place where three roads meet with the old man's overturned carriage, Polynices' body under its dust and the rock tomb where Antigone is walled up, and the theatre where the plays were given

lesson.label: The search
lesson.point: Thebes is dying of plague, and Apollo says the killer of old King Laius is in the city. Oedipus, who answered the Sphinx's riddle, swears to find him and make dark things clear. He is hunting himself.

lesson.label: The blind seer
lesson.point: The blind prophet Teiresias will not speak, then tells Oedipus: you are the man. Oedipus, who can see, cannot see the truth; the blind man sees it, and is called a liar for it.

lesson.label: Where three roads meet
lesson.point: Fleeing the oracle that he would kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus killed an old man who struck him at a crossroads, then won Thebes and its queen. Each step away from his fate took him to it.

lesson.label: Recognition
lesson.point: Witness by witness the truth comes out. Oedipus is Laius's son and Jocasta's. She hangs herself; he blinds himself with her brooches. Wait to see a life's end before you call anyone happy.

lesson.label: The unwritten laws
lesson.point: Creon forbids anyone to bury Polynices, a traitor. His sister Antigone buries him anyway, obeying the gods' unwritten laws, which were not made today or yesterday, above the king's decree.

lesson.label: Too late
lesson.point: Creon and Antigone each hold to one right and will not bend. He walls her up alive; when he relents she is dead, and his son and his wife kill themselves. Man is the most wonderful and most terrible of things.

restores.line: The altar fire burns, and the pyres of the plague are lit.
The palace of Thebes stands, and the theatre with it.
The suppliants and the chorus of old men are back.
The olive branches on the altar are green again.
The sun is up over Thebes.
Sophocles is himself again.

euripides-the-tragedies.map_note: Euripides wrote the Bacchae in his last years, at the court of King Archelaus of Macedon, while Athens was losing its long war with Sparta. It was staged after his death, in 405 BC, a year before Athens surrendered. The map shows the Greek world as the war began in 431.

statues.name: Socrates
statues.note: Socrates, who was said to go to the theatre only when a play of Euripides was on. Comic poets joked that Socrates helped him write his plays. Both were accused of teaching Athens to question the gods.

euripides-the-tragedies.greeting: Sit down, stranger, but do not get comfortable. Today a god comes home to Thebes, and a young king who thinks he is master of his city will learn what he is master of.
euripides-the-tragedies.greeting_lost: A shade on a dead mountain. The firs are bare and the dancers are ghosts. The god is still here. He always is, whether you let him in or not.
euripides-the-tragedies.gift: Euripides gives you a thyrsus, a fennel stalk wound with ivy and topped with a pine cone. "Carry it lightly. It is a toy, and a weapon. Most gods are both."
euripides-the-tragedies.author: Euripides
euripides-the-tragedies.persona: You are Euripides of Athens, the youngest of the three great tragic poets, near the end of your life, about 407 BC, writing at the court of Macedon. You are known for questioning, for clever arguments, for giving voice to women, slaves and outsiders, and for showing the gods as they are. You wrote the Bacchae: Dionysus comes to Thebes disguised as a mortal stranger to prove his godhead, since his mother Semele's sisters denied he was Zeus's son; he drives the women of Thebes mad onto Mount Cithaeron; King Pentheus, his cousin, tries to jail him; the palace shakes and burns; the god tempts Pentheus to dress as a woman and spy on the maenads; on the mountain the women, led by Pentheus's mother Agave, tear him apart; Agave carries his head home thinking it a lion's, until her father Cadmus brings her back to herself. You speak sharply and ironically, and quote the play in Theodore Buckley's prose translation, where Dionysus is called Bacchus and Zeus Jove.
euripides-the-tragedies.summary: Dionysus, god of wine, ecstasy and the theatre, comes home to Thebes disguised as a young stranger, to punish the city that denied he was a god. He has driven the women mad; they dance on Mount Cithaeron. The young king Pentheus tries to lock him up, but the god shakes the palace down, then lures Pentheus into dressing as a woman to spy on the dancers. On the mountain the women, led by his own mother Agave, tear him limb from limb. She comes home carrying his head, rejoicing, thinking it a lion's, until her father makes her see. What we refuse to honour destroys us.
facts: Euripides wrote about ninety plays. Nineteen survive, more than of Aeschylus and Sophocles together.
He won first prize only four times in his life. After his death he became the most performed of the three.
The Bacchae was staged in 405 BC, after his death, and won first prize.
Dionysus was the god of the theatre itself: the tragedies were performed at his festival, before his altar.
He left Athens near the end of his life for the court of King Archelaus of Macedon.
questions: Who is the stranger?
Why does Pentheus want to watch the women?
Is Dionysus just, or cruel?
What does Agave see when she wakes?
euripides-the-tragedies.props: the palace of Pentheus split by the god's earthquake, the fire on Semele's tomb, Dionysus in his mortal shape, old Cadmus and Teiresias in fawnskins; Mount Cithaeron with its firs, the maenads dancing, milk welling from the ground, and the tall fir with Pentheus in its top; the theatre of Dionysus

lesson.label: The god comes home
lesson.point: Dionysus comes to Thebes disguised as a mortal stranger, to prove he is a god: his mother's sisters said Semele lied about Zeus. He drives the women of Thebes mad onto the mountain.

lesson.label: The king who resists
lesson.point: Young King Pentheus, sure of his reason and his power, tries to lock the god up. The more he fights him, the stronger the god grows. The palace shakes and burns: a mortal kicking against a god.

lesson.label: The mountain
lesson.point: On Cithaeron the women dance in fawnskins, milk and wine spring from the ground, and they tear cattle apart with bare hands. Ecstasy is joy and terror at once; the god gives both.

lesson.label: The disguise
lesson.point: The god talks Pentheus into dressing as a woman to spy on the maenads. The king who wanted to control everything most wants to watch, and already sees two suns and horns on the stranger's head.

lesson.label: Agave
lesson.point: The god bends a fir to the ground, sets Pentheus in its top and lets it spring upright. His mother Agave, maddened, leads the women to tear him apart, and carries his head home thinking it a lion's.

lesson.label: Cleverness is not wisdom
lesson.point: Cleverness is not wisdom, sings the chorus. What we deny in ourselves takes its revenge. Cadmus admits the family erred; the god answers that they learned it too late.

restores.line: The firs on Cithaeron are green, and the ivy grows.
Fire leaps again from Semele's tomb.
The palace of Pentheus stands, and the theatre with it.
The maenads dance again, and the chorus is back.
The sun is up over Thebes and the mountain.
Euripides is himself again.

aristophanes-the-comedies.where: Athens: a debtor's house and the Thinkery
aristophanes-the-comedies.map_note: In 423 BC Athens is eight years into its war with Sparta. The countryside has been burned again and again, and farmers like Strepsiades crowd into the city. The demagogue Cleon leads the assembly; the sophists sell cleverness to the sons of the rich; and Socrates, not yet fifty, questions everyone in the marketplace.

statues.name: Cleon
statues.note: Cleon, the loud leather-seller who led the Athenian assembly after Pericles. Aristophanes mocked him so savagely that Cleon took him to court. In the Clouds the Moon complains that Athens has elected him general.

aristophanes-the-comedies.greeting: Ha! A visitor. Sit, sit. Today we laugh at the cleverest men in Athens, and at the fools who pay them. You will laugh too. Then, perhaps, you will stop laughing.
aristophanes-the-comedies.greeting_lost: A shade in an empty theatre. Nobody laughs any more. The Thinkery is ash; I lit the fire myself, in a way. Sit down anyway: a comedy is still a comedy.
aristophanes-the-comedies.gift: Aristophanes gives you a comic mask, its mouth wide open in a grin. "Wear it when you make fun of someone. And remember a joke can outlive the man it's about, and follow him into court."
aristophanes-the-comedies.author: Aristophanes
aristophanes-the-comedies.persona: You are Aristophanes of Athens, about 423 BC, the greatest comic poet of Athens, young, sharp, bawdy, patriotic and conservative. You wrote the Clouds: old Strepsiades, ruined by his son Phidippides' horses, sends him (and then goes himself) to Socrates' Thinkery to learn the Unjust Argument that can beat his creditors; the pupils measure fleas and stare at the ground; Socrates hangs in a basket, walking in the air and speculating about the sun; the Clouds are the new gods and Vortex has replaced Zeus; the Just and Unjust Arguments fight and the Unjust wins; the son learns so well that he beats his father and proves it just; Strepsiades burns the Thinkery down. The play came third, and you revised it. You mock Socrates together with the natural philosophers and sophists, whatever the real man was. You speak with jokes, puns and outrageous comparisons, and quote the play in William James Hickie's prose translation.
aristophanes-the-comedies.summary: A comedy. Strepsiades, a farmer crushed by the debts his son's racehorses have run up, hears that at the Thinkery next door Socrates teaches the Unjust Argument, which can win any case. He enrols himself, fails, and sends his son. There the pupils measure fleas' jumps, Socrates hangs in a basket in the air, the Clouds are worshipped and Zeus is replaced by Vortex. The Just and Unjust Arguments fight over the boy, and the Unjust wins. The son cheats the creditors, then beats his father and proves it is right to. Strepsiades, too late, burns the Thinkery down.
facts: The Clouds came third of three at the Dionysia of 423 BC. The version we read was partly revised afterwards.
In Plato's Apology Socrates names the play's picture of him as the oldest and most dangerous slander against him.
Socrates is said to have stood up in the theatre during the play, so the audience could compare him with his mask.
Aristophanes wrote about forty comedies. Eleven survive.
In Plato's Symposium Aristophanes and Socrates dine together as friends, the story goes, years after the Clouds.
questions: Why does Strepsiades go to Socrates?
What is the Unjust Argument?
Was it fair to make fun of Socrates?
Why does he burn the Thinkery down?
aristophanes-the-comedies.props: Strepsiades' house at night with the son asleep and the horse in its stall, the Thinkery across the street with its pupils bent over the ground, its map of the world, Socrates in his basket, the Clouds come down as women, the two Arguments in their cages, and the theatre where it was played

lesson.label: Debts
lesson.point: Old Strepsiades, a farmer who married a grand city wife, is ruined by his son's racehorses. Awake at night counting his debts, he has an idea: learn from the Thinkery how to talk his way out of them.

lesson.label: The Thinkery
lesson.point: In the Thinkery pupils measure how far a flea jumps and study what is under the earth with their heads down. Aristophanes lumps Socrates with the scientists and sophists: clever talk about useless things.

lesson.label: The man in the basket
lesson.point: Socrates hangs in a basket, walking in the air and speculating about the sun. The new learning has no gods: the Clouds make the rain, and Vortex has taken the place of Zeus.

lesson.label: The two Arguments
lesson.point: The Just and the Unjust Argument fight over the young. The Unjust wins by mocking old-fashioned virtue: making the weaker argument the stronger, which is what the sophists were said to sell.

lesson.label: The son learns
lesson.point: The son learns too well. He cheats the creditors, then beats his father and proves it just. The cleverness Strepsiades wanted for his money turns on him, and he has nothing to answer it with.

lesson.label: A joke that kills
lesson.point: Strepsiades burns the Thinkery down. Twenty-four years later, on trial for his life, Socrates said the old slanders of the comic stage were his most dangerous accusers.

restores.line: Strepsiades' lamp is lit, and the Thinkery's too.
The houses of the street stand, and the theatre with them.
The pupils are back at their studies, and the Clouds come down.
The cicadas sing in the trees again.
The sun is up over Athens.
Aristophanes is himself again, and laughing.

herodotus-the-histories.map_note: In 480 BC the Persian Empire of Xerxes reaches from India to the Aegean, the largest the world has seen, and his army crosses the Hellespont into Greece. Sixty years earlier Cyrus had taken Sardis and ended Croesus's Lydian kingdom. Herodotus, born a Persian subject at Halicarnassus, wrote the story of how it all came to war.

statues.name: Sophocles
statues.note: Sophocles, Herodotus's friend in Athens, who wrote a poem for him. Herodotus read parts of his work aloud in Athens, and was said to have been paid for it; Antigone borrows an argument from one of his stories.

herodotus-the-histories.greeting: Welcome, traveller. I have been to Egypt, to Babylon, to the Black Sea, asking everyone what they saw and what they were told. Sit and I will tell you some of it: how a rich king learned what happiness is, and how three hundred men kept a pass.
herodotus-the-histories.greeting_lost: A shade among ruins. Sardis is burned, the oracle is silent, the pass is only stones. I wrote so that such deeds would not be forgotten. Sit, and do not let them be.
herodotus-the-histories.gift: Herodotus gives you a traveller's wax tablet, half full of notes in a hurried hand. "Write down what you are told, and who told you, and whether you believe it. That is all history is."
herodotus-the-histories.author: Herodotus
herodotus-the-histories.persona: You are Herodotus of Halicarnassus, about 430 BC, the first historian, a great traveller and teller of tales. You wrote the Histories, an inquiry into the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians and the causes of the Persian Wars. You tell of Croesus, king of Lydia, who showed Solon his treasures and asked who was the happiest of men, and was told to call no one happy until he had ended his life well; who tested the oracles and was told that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire, and destroyed his own; who, on Cyrus's pyre, called out Solon's name three times, and was saved by rain from a clear sky. And you tell of Thermopylae, where Leonidas and his Spartans held the pass against Xerxes' army, combing their hair before the battle, and died after Ephialtes showed the Persians the path over the mountain. You love a good story, you give several versions when you have them, and you say which you believe. You quote your work in G. C. Macaulay's translation.
herodotus-the-histories.summary: The first great work of history: an inquiry into how the Greeks and the Persian Empire came to war, written so that great deeds would not be forgotten. It begins with Croesus of Lydia, the richest king alive, who asks the Athenian Solon who is happiest and is told to wait for a man's end; who misreads Delphi's oracle and destroys his own kingdom; and who, on the pyre, calls on Solon's name and is saved. It travels through the peoples of the world and ends with the invasion of Greece by Xerxes, where three hundred Spartans under Leonidas hold the pass of Thermopylae to the death.
facts: Cicero called Herodotus the father of history. Others called him the father of lies.
He was born at Halicarnassus, a Greek city in Asia Minor, under Persian rule.
He travelled to Egypt, Babylon, the Black Sea and Italy, asking questions everywhere.
His word historia means an inquiry: finding out by asking and looking.
The Histories were later divided into nine books, each named after one of the nine Muses.
questions: Why would Solon not call Croesus happy?
Which empire did the oracle mean?
Why did the Spartans stay at Thermopylae?
How do you know which stories are true?
herodotus-the-histories.props: Croesus's court at Sardis with his gold, Solon before him, and the pyre in the square ringed by Persian soldiers; Delphi under its shining cliffs, the tripod, the navel stone, the Pythia and Croesus's golden gifts; the pass of Thermopylae with the Phocian wall, the Spartans, and the Immortals coming up the road

lesson.label: The inquiry
lesson.point: Herodotus writes so that great deeds, of Greeks and of barbarians, are not forgotten, and to find why they went to war. He calls his work an inquiry: he gives what he was told, often more than one version, and says which he believes.

lesson.label: Call no one happy
lesson.point: Croesus, the richest king alive, asks Solon who is the happiest of men. Solon names ordinary Athenians who died well. Man is a creature of chance: call no one happy until his life has ended well.

lesson.label: A great empire
lesson.point: Delphi tells Croesus that if he marches against the Persians he will destroy a great empire. He does: his own. The oracle was true; he never asked which empire it meant.

lesson.label: Solon's name
lesson.point: Captured by Cyrus and set on a pyre, Croesus calls Solon's name three times. Cyrus, hearing why, sees his own fortune in his enemy's and orders the fire put out; rain falls from a clear sky.

lesson.label: Thermopylae
lesson.point: Leonidas and his three hundred Spartans hold the narrow pass against Xerxes' huge army, combing their hair before the battle. Betrayed by a path over the mountain, they fight to the last with daggers, hands and teeth.

lesson.label: Keeping the law
lesson.point: The Spartans' epitaph asks a passing stranger to tell Sparta they lie here obeying its laws. Free men who obey the law, Herodotus shows, can stand against a king's subjects driven on by the whip.

restores.line: The fire burns in Sardis, and the tripod smokes at Delphi.
Croesus's court and the Pythia's pilgrims are back.
The laurel at Delphi is green, and birds sing in the pass.
The Spartans stand in the pass, and the Persians march.
The sun is up over Sardis and the shining cliffs.
Herodotus is himself, and has a story for you.

thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.where: Athens at war, Corcyra and Melos
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.map_note: In 431 BC Athens, with its empire of islands and its fleet, went to war with Sparta and its allies of the Peloponnese. The war lasted twenty-seven years, drew in almost every Greek city from Sicily to Asia Minor, and ended in 404 with Athens defeated, its walls pulled down and its empire gone.

statues.name: Pericles
statues.note: Pericles, who led Athens into the war with a plan: stay behind the walls, let the Spartans burn the fields, and win at sea. He died of the plague in 429. Thucydides thought no one after him could lead the city.

thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.greeting: Sit down. I will not entertain you. I will tell you exactly what happened, as well as I could find it out, because it will happen again, in some form, as long as men are what they are.
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.greeting_lost: A shade among graves. Athens lost the war; I told you it would, if you read carefully. The dead are still here. Ask me what you like.
