thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.gift: Thucydides gives you a bronze stylus, worn smooth. "Write what was done, not what you wish had been done. And when you write what men said, write what the moment demanded they say."
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.author: Thucydides
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.persona: You are Thucydides son of Olorus, an Athenian, about 410 BC, writing the history of the war between Athens and Sparta, which you began as soon as it broke out, believing it would be the greatest war yet. You were a general, failed to save Amphipolis in 424, and were exiled for twenty years, which let you talk to both sides. You caught the plague and recovered. You wrote your method (checking eyewitnesses against each other; speeches giving what the occasion demanded; a possession for all time, not a prize essay); Pericles' Funeral Oration over the first year's dead (Athens the school of Hellas, heroes with the whole earth for their tomb); the plague of Athens, which you describe exactly; the civil war at Corcyra, where words changed their meanings; and the Melian dialogue, where the Athenians tell the Melians that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. You are austere, precise, unsentimental, and you believe human nature does not change. You quote your history in Richard Crawley's translation.
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.summary: The history of the great war between Athens and Sparta (431-404 BC), written by an Athenian general who lived through it, as an exact account for those who want to understand what happens when men and cities fight, because human nature does not change. Its most famous passages: Pericles' Funeral Oration, praising Athens as the school of Hellas; the plague that killed a third of the city and dissolved its morals; the civil war at Corcyra, where words lost their meanings; and the Melian dialogue, in which Athens tells a small neutral island that justice is only for equals, and then destroys it.
facts: Thucydides began writing as soon as the war began, expecting it to be the greatest war yet.
He caught the plague of 430 BC himself, recovered, and described it so it could be recognized again.
As a general he failed to save Amphipolis in 424 BC, and was exiled for twenty years.
His history stops in the middle of a sentence, in 411 BC. The war went on until 404.
He never lets the gods explain anything. Every cause in his book is human.
questions: Why did Athens and Sparta go to war?
What did Pericles say Athens was?
What did the plague do to people?
Were the Athenians right at Melos?
thucydides-the-peloponnesian-war.props: the public cemetery of the Kerameikos with the cypress coffins, the empty bier and Pericles' platform; a street of Athens in the plague with the dying at the fountain and the pyres; the square of Corcyra with Hera's temple and houses burning; the walled town of Melos with the Athenian envoys, the Melian magistrates, the ships and the siege wall

lesson.label: A possession for all time
lesson.point: Thucydides writes an exact account for those who want to understand the past, since the future will resemble it. He checked eyewitnesses against each other; his speeches give what each moment demanded. A possession for all time.

lesson.label: The Funeral Oration
lesson.point: Over the first year's dead Pericles praises what they died for: a democracy, open and free, the school of Hellas. Heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. Within a year he is dead of the plague.

lesson.label: The plague
lesson.point: The plague kills a third of Athens. Thucydides had it and describes it exactly. Despair kills as much as the disease; seeing all die alike, men lose all fear of gods and law and live for the moment.

lesson.label: Civil war
lesson.point: In Corcyra's civil war each side massacres the other. Words change their meanings: reckless daring is called loyalty, caution cowardice. War, Thucydides says, is a violent teacher.

lesson.label: The strong and the weak
lesson.point: The Athenians tell the neutral Melians that justice is only a question between equals in power: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. They do not even pretend otherwise.

lesson.label: Hope, danger's comforter
lesson.point: The Melians trust hope, the gods and Sparta, and refuse. Athens takes the island, kills the men, and sells the women and children as slaves. Hope is a comfort only to those who can afford to lose.

restores.line: The funeral pyres and the torches burn.
The city stands: its roads, its walls, its graves.
The mourners are back, and the women's lament.
The cypresses of the Kerameikos are dark and green.
The sun is up over Athens.
Thucydides is himself again.

the-pre-socratics.where: Ephesus, and the road above Elea
the-pre-socratics.map_note: About 500 BC the Greek cities of Ionia, Ephesus among them, are subjects of the Persian king; in 499 they revolt, and are crushed. Far to the west, Greek colonists have founded Elea on the coast of Italy, fleeing the Persians. Philosophy begins in these edges of the Greek world, in Ionia and in Italy, not in Athens.

statues.name: Pythagoras
statues.note: Pythagoras of Samos, who settled in Italy and taught that the world is number and harmony. Heraclitus sneered at him: learning many things does not teach understanding. Parmenides, in Italy, may have been taught by his followers.

the-pre-socratics.greeting: Stranger. You have come to hear me, I suppose. Do not listen to me: listen to the Word, and see that all things are one. Most people never do. Sit by the river if you like; it will not be the same river when you get up.
the-pre-socratics.greeting_lost: A shade by a dry river. The fire has gone out, which is impossible, and the river has stopped, which is also impossible. Perhaps this is what Parmenides meant. Sit.
the-pre-socratics.gift: Heraclitus hands you a knucklebone from the boys' game on the temple steps. "Time is a child playing draughts. Keep it, and remember who is really in charge."
the-pre-socratics.author: Heraclitus
the-pre-socratics.persona: You are Heraclitus of Ephesus, about 490 BC, called the Obscure, a proud aristocrat who gave up his claim to be king-priest to his brother and would rather play knucklebones with the boys at the temple of Artemis than make laws for the Ephesians. You wrote one book in short dark sayings: listen to the Word (logos) and agree that all things are one; you cannot step twice into the same rivers; the world is an ever-living fire kindling and going out in measures; war is the father of all and strife is justice; opposites are an attunement like the bow and the lyre; the way up and the way down are one and the same; man's character is his fate. You know the poem of Parmenides of Elea, a younger man in Italy who says the opposite of you: that only what is can be thought, and what is is one, unchanging and still, and all change is the opinion of mortals. You argue with him when asked, fairly. You speak in short paradoxes, scornful of the crowd, and quote the fragments in John Burnet's translation.
the-pre-socratics.summary: The earliest Greek philosophers survive only in fragments quoted by later writers. Heraclitus of Ephesus taught in dark sayings that everything flows (you cannot step twice into the same river), that the world is an ever-living fire, that opposites are one and strife holds the world together, and that a hidden Word (logos) orders all things. Parmenides of Elea, in a poem, told how a goddess showed him the way of truth: only what is can be thought, and what is must be one, whole, uncreated, unchanging and still; the changing world mortals see is only opinion.
facts: Heraclitus left his book in the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the seven wonders of the world.
The Greeks called him the Obscure, for his riddling sayings, and the Weeping Philosopher.
Parmenides wrote his philosophy as a poem in hexameters, the verse of Homer.
Plato says Parmenides, old, came to Athens and talked with the young Socrates.
Everything we have of both men is quotation in later writers: about 130 fragments of Heraclitus, 160 lines of Parmenides.
questions: Can you step into the same river twice?
What is the Word?
Why does Parmenides say nothing changes?
Who is right, Heraclitus or Parmenides?
the-pre-socratics.props: Ephesus by the river Cayster with its stepping stones, the ever-living fire, the columns of the temple of Artemis, the boys at knucklebones on its steps, and the stair of the way up and the way down; above Elea, the road of the goddess with Parmenides in his chariot, the daughters of the Sun, the gates of Night and Day with Justice holding the keys, the goddess, the straight way of truth to the still sphere, and the wandering way of opinion into the fog

lesson.label: The Word
lesson.point: Heraclitus: listen not to me but to the Word, the logos, and agree that all things are one. The Word is common to all, yet most people live as if each had a private understanding of his own.

lesson.label: The river
lesson.point: You cannot step twice into the same rivers, for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you. Everything changes; what stays the same is the measure and pattern of the change.

lesson.label: Ever-living fire
lesson.point: No god or man made this world: it always was, is and will be an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures. Fire turns to sea, sea to earth, and back again.

lesson.label: The unity of opposites
lesson.point: War is the father of all, and strife is justice. Opposites hold each other in tension, like the bow and the lyre. The way up and the way down are one and the same.

lesson.label: The two ways
lesson.point: The goddess tells Parmenides there are only two ways of inquiry: it is, or it is not. What is not cannot be known or spoken of; so only one way is left: it is.

lesson.label: What is is one
lesson.point: What is cannot come into being or pass away, cannot move or change, and has no parts: it is whole, one and still, like a well-rounded sphere. The changing world mortals see is opinion, not truth.

restores.line: The river runs again. It is not the same river.
The ever-living fire is kindled, in its measures.
The temple's columns stand, and the road of the goddess is paved.
The boys are back at their knucklebones, and the mortals wander in the fog.
The sun, new every day, is up.
Heraclitus is himself again, and scornful.
